title: Sort with comparator
description: `.sort()` MUTATES and defaults to STRING comparison. Always pass a comparator for numbers.

notes: .sort MUTATES the original array. Use `[...arr].sort()` if you need a copy.
Default sort converts to string, so `[10, 2, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 2]`.
Comparator returns negative → a first, positive → b first, 0 → equal (order preserved on stable sorts).

questions.q: A comparator returning a negative number means:
You need the sorted result but must NOT change the original array. Which is correct?
questions.explain: `.sort()` mutates in place, so copy first with `[...arr]` (or `arr.slice()`); there is no non-mutating `.sorted()` on arrays.

questions.q: You write `(a, b) => a > b` as a numeric comparator. What's the bug?
options: It returns a boolean (true/false), which coerces to 1/0 — it never returns a negative, so the sort order is unreliable
questions.explain: A comparator must return negative/zero/positive; `a > b` yields true/false → 1/0, never negative, so equal-or-less cases are indistinguishable and ordering is broken.

questions.q: Two objects compare equal under your comparator. A 'stable' sort guarantees what about them?
options: Their relative order from the input is preserved
They are placed at the end
questions.explain: Stability means equal elements keep their original relative order — modern V8 `.sort()` is stable, which matters when sorting by a secondary key after a primary one.

L3.prompt: Write `sortByAge(arr)` returning the array sorted by `.age` ascending. Log `JSON.stringify(sortByAge([{name:"A",age:30},{name:"B",age:25}]))`.
